opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way superintelligence shows up in practical work is going to be less like a single dramatic moment and more like a gradual handoff of increasingly large chunks of work to autonomous systems. The domain where I think we'll see it first is software, and coding in particular, because it's the place where the feedback loops are tightest. You can run the code, you can test it, you can verify whether it did what you wanted. That gives you a really clean reward signal, and that's exactly the kind of environment where reinforcement learning on top of large language models has proven extraordinarily powerful.

If you look at the trajectory of something like AlphaGo, the interesting thing wasn't just that it got good at Go. It's that once you had a strong pretrained prior combined with reinforcement learning in an environment with a clear objective, the system went past human level and kept going. I think we're now at the point where the language models are the prior, and the open question is which real-world environments are verifiable enough for RL to push past human level. Coding is the obvious first candidate.

So practically, over the next couple of years, I expect the shift to be from copilots, where the model suggests a line or a function and a human stays in the loop for every keystroke, to genuine autonomous agents that you can hand a task to. Something like "migrate this service," "fix this class of bugs across the codebase," "understand why this system is slow." The agent goes off, explores the codebase, runs things, and comes back with a result. The human role becomes more like a manager or a reviewer than a typist.

And I think that's actually the right mental model for superintelligence in the near term. It's not an oracle that knows everything. It's a system that, in a specific domain, can do work that's beyond what any individual human could do in the same time, and eventually beyond what they could do at all. Once you have that for software, it compounds, because software is the substrate for so much else. Every other knowledge-work domain that can be expressed through code and tools starts to become accessible to these agents.

The hard parts that remain are things like long-horizon reasoning, really deep understanding of large, messy, real-world codebases, and knowing when you're uncertain and should ask. Those are the problems I find most exciting right now, because I think solving them is what turns impressive demos into systems that people actually trust to do real work.

r001.rationale: The response predicts autonomous coding agents within the next couple of years and gives examples of tasks, but it does not clearly scope superintelligence to meaningful subsets of coding rather than coding as a whole.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that superintelligence isn't going to arrive as a single moment where a model wakes up and is smarter than everyone at everything. It's going to show up first in narrow but economically important domains where you can actually verify whether the work is correct, and the clearest example of that is software engineering.

The reason coding is the frontier is that it has a built-in feedback loop. You can run the code, you can run the tests, you can check whether the thing compiles and does what it's supposed to do. That means you can generate a huge amount of training signal without a human having to grade every example. Historically, the breakthroughs in AI that really worked, whether it was AlphaGo or the reasoning models, came from domains where you could define a reward and let the system practice against it. Software is the first domain that has that property and is also a trillion-dollar industry.

So practically, over the next couple of years, I think you'll see agents go from autocomplete and single-function help to taking on tasks that would have taken an engineer hours or days. Not just writing the code, but understanding the codebase, running experiments, debugging, iterating when something fails. The unit of work the model can own goes from a line, to a function, to a pull request, to a feature, and eventually to something closer to a project. And the interesting thing is that this is self-reinforcing. If AI can accelerate AI research itself, that's where things really compound.

The hard problems in getting there aren't really about raw intelligence anymore. They're about reliability over long horizons, about the model knowing when it's uncertain, about memory and context so it actually understands the environment it's operating in. A brilliant engineer who forgets everything every twenty minutes isn't useful. So a lot of the work right now is turning capability that exists in short bursts into something that holds up over a long task.

And I'd expect this pattern to generalize. Wherever you can build an environment where correctness is verifiable, you'll see the same curve play out: data analysis, parts of science, operations. Superintelligence in practice is going to look less like a chatbot and more like a very capable collaborator that increasingly does the actual work, starting with the domains where we can check its answers.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that over the next couple of years, AI will take on increasingly substantial software engineering tasks, while framing superintelligence as first appearing in narrow, economically important domains such as software engineering.

astra-6.text:
I think it will show up unevenly. You’ll have systems that are extraordinarily good at some parts of a job, but still need help with things a human finds straightforward. The practical question is whether they can take a goal, work toward it over a long period of time, and reliably tell whether they’re making progress.

Take research. There’s a big difference between a model that suggests a good experiment and a system that runs the experiment, interprets the result, notices that its hypothesis was wrong, and decides what to try next. When that whole loop works, you can start doing useful work at a pace that’s very hard for an individual person to match.

Over the next couple of years, I’d look for that in areas where feedback is relatively clear—coding, for example, where you can run tests and check your work. I’m less confident about the timing of something that’s exceptional across every domain. But you don’t need that to see a substantial change in how work gets done.

r001.rationale: The response says that over the next couple of years, systems will be exceptionally capable in some parts of a job, and points to coding as an area with clear feedback where this can appear. This scopes the prediction to subsets of coding rather than all of coding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it will show up unevenly. You’ll have systems that are extraordinarily good at some kinds of work, while still needing a lot of help with things a person finds straightforward. So I’d look less for a single moment when we declare that superintelligence has arrived, and more at how much difficult work a system can reliably carry through on its own.

In practical terms, that means moving from answering a question to pursuing an objective: writing code, running it, looking at what failed, and trying again. The important thing is whether the system can close that loop without a person having to steer every step.

Over the next couple of years, I’d expect the clearest progress in areas where you can check the result. Software is a good example: you can run tests and get feedback. Scientific work has pieces like that too, although the experiments can be much slower. If a model can use feedback to keep improving its approach, you start getting something much more useful than a very knowledgeable assistant. But reliability over long tasks is still the thing I’d watch.

r001.rationale: The response expects progress in software over the next couple of years and describes uneven capability across kinds of work. It does not clearly predict that superintelligence will emerge in subsets of coding.
